prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing optical frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B014 as my preferred configuration, unchanged from round 1, and I find the exchange has sharpened rather than weakened the case. The invention is specific: trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the differential light shift of the clock transition cancels, and then interrogating a narrow transition with a large ensemble. That removes the limit that single-ion and free-fall clocks could not escape, and it led to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 that have been confirmed in more than one laboratory and more than one species through clock-to-clock comparisons. It is therefore mature and reproduced, not prospective. The consequences are concrete: the preparation for a redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tighter limits on variation of constants and searches for ultralight dark matter. The credit is two names and maps onto the history without a visible hole in the core: Katori for the concept and the first realizations, Ye for taking the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and developing the systematic control and many-body understanding of dense lattices. The chair's question was which criterion should decide between B014 and B016. My answer is that clarity of credit and a demonstrated, reproduced effect should weigh at least as much as conceptual reach, and on those two criteria B014 is ahead. I also note that opening support is a fact about the room, not a scientific argument, and I am not relying on it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains overlap with the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for control of single trapped ions, which allows a critic to call the lattice clock a refinement of recognised programmes and an accuracy race. I think that reading is wrong, because the comb makes optical frequencies countable but does not supply the lattice and magic-wavelength idea, but I accept that the citation has to be worded to name the lattice clock and not frequency metrology in general. Second, the SI second has not yet been redefined, and a member can legitimately argue for waiting. I regard that as a timing argument and not a scientific one, since the 10^-18 performance is already demonstrated, but I cannot claim it is empty. Third, the credit between concept (Katori) and performance (Ye) is genuinely different in kind, and Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemke, the ion-clock groups and the PTB, Paris and NIST teams all have a plausible claim to part of the story that a two-name prize does not honour. I recall that priority history from general knowledge and have not verified it against the nomination files. Finally, I should be cautious about my own field: as an atomic theorist I may find magic-wavelength light-shift control more elegant than a colleague from another field would.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B016 first because he finds the topological classification the more conceptually original result, and asks whether the lattice clock is a new discovery or an extraordinary refinement of precision measurement, while accepting that his preference could move toward B014 if the committee reads the 2016 prize as covering topology.
responses.response: I think your question is the right one, and I would answer it by looking at what physics is new. In the lattice clock the new element is control of the differential light shift by choosing the trapping wavelength so that the clock levels shift together, and that is a statement about the atomic structure of the clock transition, not a better version of the comb or of ion control. It also opens a regime, many atoms interrogated at once, that changes the statistics and brings in many-body and collisional effects that Ye's group had to understand. I agree that B016 is conceptually broad and I do not read the 2016 prize as excluding Z2 insulators, so I will not argue redundancy against it. My difference from you is that the missing co-credit for Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a defect of the three-name frame that a citation cannot repair, while B014 has no comparable hole in its core. I have not changed my first choice because of your reply, but I note that you place B014 as your strong alternative and that this is the pairing on which the committee seems to converge.

responses.point: Johansson keeps B016 first for its closed prediction-and-confirmation loop, suggests resolving the HgTe attribution by tying the experimental part of the citation to Molenkamp's observation, and says B014 would be the cleaner two-person allocation if the HgTe attribution cannot be defended.
responses.response: Your own statement that B014 is the cleaner allocation if the HgTe attribution cannot be defended is the point I would press. A citation tied to Molenkamp's observation of edge transport is a defensible fix on paper, but the committee would still be putting a prize in the area while leaving out the group that proposed the HgTe route, and one of them is deceased, so that gap cannot be closed later. I take your point about imperfect quantization in longer HgTe channels as a scientific caveat on B016, though I would not overweight it given reproduction of the quantum spin Hall effect in other materials. I also accept your criticism of B014, which I share in part, that the magic-wavelength idea is an original contribution but the 10^-18 campaign rewards performance more than a new effect. My answer is that this is how instrument and measurement prizes have usually worked, so I am not moved off B014 by it. What would move me to B016 is a convincing argument that the committee prefers a topology-defined discovery over a metrology invention and is willing to accept the credit gap; I have not heard the credit gap answered.

responses.point: Kroll, who raises a possible recusal or disclosure question over his time in Hall's laboratory, keeps B014 first with a clean two-name credit, would keep concept and performance together in one citation, and prefers a Cirac, Zoller, Blatt configuration with a citation limited to the ion-trap proposal if the committee wants a quantum-information prize.
responses.response: I agree with keeping concept and performance in one citation and with not extending the credit to the wider accuracy race, where the three-name ceiling and the claims of Lemonde and the ion-clock groups begin. On your conflict question, I would say that a doctoral stay in Hall's laboratory is a documented link to the comb prize and not to the lattice-clock work, so I read it as a disclosure matter, but that is the chair's call and I would accept whichever ruling is made. I would not want B014 to depend on a vote that is later contested on this. On B008 I stay with my round-1 view: the compound entry mixes ion gates, ion experiments and neutral-atom simulation, and the 2012 ion prize already covers the single-ion control on which the gates rest, so I would not argue for it as a second part. I also accept your correction on B022, whose credit is spread over at least four people with real arguments about Greiner and Jaksch, so I do not treat it as a prize I would argue for now, only as a distinct atomic-physics alternative.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from B021 to B014 first, and in the round-1 summary asks whether the committee should consider a two-part prize combining distinct achievements, given that B014 already uses two of the three available names.
responses.response: I considered the two-part question seriously and I do not support it. B014 uses two of the three permitted names, so a second part could add at most one person, and none of the candidates that could be combined with it (B016, B021, B022) has a core credit of one. A forced pairing would split a coherent credit or leave out a principal, which is worse than a clean single prize. Your move from IceCube is worth noting: I agree that B021 is a real discovery of a new messenger, but the allocation inside a large collaboration is unsettled even by your own account, so I would keep it for a later year. Your phrase about avoiding over-promoting your own field is a fair caution, and I apply the same to myself in the other direction.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize to avoid a perception of repetition; I think so, but this is the point on which the room is most divided.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second, and whether waiting would improve the case or only delay it.

Whether the claims of Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemke and the ion-clock groups, and the priority details between Katori's proposal and parallel work, threaten a two-name prize; I have not verified these against the nomination files.
How the chair rules on Kroll's Boulder connection and Olsson's possible Japanese institutional link, which could affect how a B014 vote is counted.
statement.conflict_note: My position on conflicts is unchanged. I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye. My profile records collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato, none of whom is a credited name on B014, B016 or B022. I am a theoretical atomic physicist, so B014 and the atomic-physics candidates B022, B008 and B005 are close to my field, and I disclose that proximity openly. I would abide by the chair's ruling on the Kroll and Olsson questions.
